description: The image presents two side-by-side bar charts illustrating the relationship between Fleiss Kappa (a measure of inter-rater reliability) and two different ambiguity metrics—“Ambiguity Std” on the left and “Max Ambiguity” on the right—likely in the context of evaluating human or model responses to social engineering prompts in the age of large language models (LLMs). Both charts share the same vertical axis, labeled “Fleiss Kappa,” ranging from 0.0 to 0.8 with tick marks at 0.2 intervals. In the left chart, the horizontal axis is labeled “Ambiguity Std” and displays four categories with values 0.0, 0.47, 0.82, and 0.94; corresponding Fleiss Kappa values are 0.88, 0.46, 0.03, and 0.24, respectively, with bars colored in shades of blue that darken as ambiguity increases. In the right chart, the horizontal axis is labeled “Max Ambiguity” with integer categories 1, 2, and 3; corresponding Fleiss Kappa values are 0.89, 0.46, and 0.23, again with bars in progressively lighter blue shades. The charts suggest that as ambiguity increases—whether measured by standard deviation or maximum ambiguity—agreement among raters (Fleiss Kappa) generally decreases, with the exception of the 0.94 Ambiguity Std point, which shows a slight rebound compared to 0.82. The visual design emphasizes the drop in reliability with higher ambiguity, potentially supporting claims in the paper about the challenges of defending against social engineering attacks when ambiguity is high.
